doc.title: Ken Peplowski interviewed by Monk Rowe, Aspen, Colorado, October 10, 1997 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Awkward pairings and all-star groups
summary: Promoters' odd combinations like Red Rodney and Jay McShann, and why all-star bands often fail.

story.theme_name: Leading a band: choosing, paying and managing players
story.community_name: Leading a band: running, choosing and keeping players

blocks.x: Just to wrap up, this weekend you’ll be playing with some pretty well-known musicians. Has there ever been any awkward moments at these? I know that the promoters, they kind of juggle people, they bring in all individuals, no bands really. And have you ever had a circumstance where the chemistry that they put together just hasn’t worked?

Yes that happens sometimes. But thankfully the sets are fairly short. I mean sometimes the promoters — this party actually I’ve seen the set list, and everything kind of works for this weekend. Because on this one, the musicians put together the sets. Jack Lesberg and Ralph Sutton do the sets. So they know who can play with who. But there were some famous ones a few years ago — I don’t know if I should mention names or not — but there was a famous promoter that almost started the jazz parties, and he used to put together the oddest combinations. Like for example I actually was at one where it was Red Rodney and Jay McShann, and things like that. And both of those people are great, but you put two people who have absolutely nothing in common, maybe one or two tunes between them, and that’s very awkward. And neither person enjoys it and they just want to get off stage as quickly as possible, with as little bloodshed as they can. But generally these things, you know it’s a pretty homogeneous group of musicians and they don’t really stretch the boundaries that much in either direction. So it’s not set up so there’s going to be that many disasters on these. But I’ve done festivals in Europe where they’ve put together these alleged all-star groups. A lot of times those don’t work because there’s all these big egos involved, and everybody is a leader, and a lot of those all-star groups don’t work.
Sometimes you wonder, gee, how come this guy never made a record with that guy — because they’re all stars.

There’s a reason for it. Because they see music differently. They’re band leaders, and they don’t want to work with that person. And unfortunately, the last person that many promoters ask about the music is the musicians. Part of this thing for them is they want to be a band leader. It’s a surrogate thing for them. They can play band leader and put these combinations together. Any time I see the word “all-star” I try to run the other way. Because usually it’s going to be a bunch of guys that are not completely happy to be there, and it turns into a pretty good jam session. The music is always better when it’s a set band and it’s people that work together all the time and play off of each other. I’m always trying to push to get my own group on these things, or play with just people I really love to play with, like Howard and Randy. And we can try to play some new things or actually bring some music up to the bandstand. And the jam sessions are fun too but if you do a lot of them they’re not as much fun for us as they are for the audience.
